_comment: op -> cell table for the bundled-data backend.  Shaped after Dynamatic's
own data/rtl-config-verilog.json (op name + parameter guards -> an
implementation), because that structure is already proven to cover this
op set.  The difference is what sits behind it: cells/rtl/, four-phase
'kind' says how an op is realised, and only these five values exist:
cells   -- instantiate the listed cells/rtl/ modules
wire    -- no cells at all; the op is rewiring (see 'why' on each)
tree    -- an N-way op built from the 2-way cell named in 'cells'
compute -- Stage 3, the generated compute-unit wrapper.  NOT YET BUILT
todo    -- Stage 6 memory.  NOT YET BUILT, and audited as unsafe to
'seen' is the number of occurrences across the four compiled kernels in
bdc/map.py --report, not estimated.  An op absent from the corpus has
seen: 0 and is mapped on the strength of the op definition alone, which
is weaker evidence; those are called out in 'why'.

control_channel_convention.spelling: W=1, data inputs tied to 0, data output left dangling
why: A handshake control channel is `<>`: req and ack, no data.  Every
data-touching cell in cells/rtl/ declares [W-1:0], and W=0 is illegal
Verilog, so a control channel cannot be spelled W=0 without changing
the library -- which is frozen.
Measured rather than assumed: bd_mux at W=8 costs 4 LUT1 + 1 LUT2 +
4 LUT6 + 4 LUT6_2.  At W=1 with the data output READ it costs the same
control logic plus one LUT3 for the 1-bit datapath.  At W=1 with the
data output DANGLING it costs 4 LUT1 + 1 LUT2 + 4 LUT6 and the LUT3 is
gone -- yosys removes the datapath when nothing reads it.
So a control channel costs exactly zero extra LUTs and needs no new
cell.  The emitter must leave the data output genuinely unread for
this to hold; connecting it to a top-level port would put the LUT3
back.
caveat: The purely-control cells -- bd_fork, bd_join, bd_steer, bd_arbiter,
bd_ctree -- have no data ports at all, so this convention never
applies to them.  It is only bd_mux, bd_link, bd_pipe, bd_src and
bd_snk that have to be told a width.

why: Data is wires: one producer's data bus fans out to N consumers with
no cell in between.  The whole cost is the ack rendezvous, which is
bd_fork's bd_ctree.
The roadmap said '+bd_ctree past fan-out 4'.  That is wrong as a
compiler obligation -- bd_fork already instantiates bd_ctree #(.N(N))
and bd_ctree recurses in chunks of four for any N.  The compiler
emits one bd_fork whatever the fan-out.
Fan-outs in the corpus: 31x[2], 15x[3], 9x[4], 3x[5], 1x[6].
Absent from the four kernels; present in Dynamatic's own tests.
Their lazy fork exists to keep two LSQ group allocations off the same
CLOCK CYCLE, a guarantee bdc/AUDIT.md section 2 records as void here.
Mapping it to bd_fork therefore drops a guarantee we could not have
honoured anyway -- acceptable only because it appears exclusively on
the memory network, which is Stage 6 and gated behind 'todo' below.
Revisit before any memory op is emitted.

ops.why: The dual of fork; not emitted by the frontend for these kernels.

why: bd_steer routes req to one of two outputs on s and collects the ack.
It has no data ports and needs none: under bundled data the data bus
runs to both destinations and only the request is steered.
No bd_bd2dr converter.  The library's rule is dual-rail only on a
control channel that arrives separately from the data it steers; here
the condition rides in the bundle, so there is no boundary to cross.

ops.why: Pure forwarding (`%11 = br %10`). A wire in a dataflow graph.

why: ALL 21 merges in the corpus have exactly one operand. A one-input
merge forwards, so it is a wire and costs nothing.
Never bd_merge.  bd_merge needs the second input to be unable to
assert until the first transaction has fully completed, and its own
header says pipelined code does not satisfy that.  Dynamatic emits
pipelined dataflow and documents merge as nondeterministic.  Full
evidence in bdc/AUDIT.md section 1.
Arbitrate unconditionally; no exclusivity analysis gates a cheaper
path.  One uniform lowering beats two with a silent-downgrade mode.
One predecessor means no decision to make: the data output is a wire
and the index output is the constant 0, which is itself wires plus a
tied-off data bus.
control_merge derives its index from WHICH input arrived, so it
cannot be selected by its own output. Something must resolve
possibly-coincident requests, and on a LUT fabric that is bd_arbiter.
10 of the 11 are 2-input and map to exactly one bd_arbiter + one
bd_mux. The remaining one is 3-input (gcd, control_merge at
handshake_transformed.mlir:239) and needs the tree construction.
operands[0] is the select, operands[1:] the data inputs. A 2-way mux
is exactly one bd_mux: select on the ctl channel, inputs on x and y.
This is the good case and it is the common one -- 25 of 26 muxes in
the corpus are 2-way. bd_mux acknowledges only the selected input and
leaves the other's token untouched, which is what a loop header
needs, and it infers nothing from a request wire.
N-way mux from 2-way cells. The one instance is gcd's 3-way mux at
handshake_transformed.mlir:238, paired with the 3-way control_merge
on the next line -- the same 3-predecessor loop header.
Unsolved detail, and the reason this is 'tree' and not 'cells': the
index is iN for N inputs but bd_mux takes a 1-bit s, so the tree
needs the index decoded into per-level selects. Exactly one op in
the corpus forces this, so it is not on the critical path to a first
running program -- test_loop_free, single_loop and fir need none.
A token forever, which is exactly bd_src (req = ~ack). Control-only,
so W=1 per the convention above.
The library states the obligation the compiler must honour: a bd_src
has no state of its own to reset, because ~x is x, so it must sit
behind a consumer that does reset. The emitter has to check that,
not assume it.
`%3 = constant %2 {value = 0 : i32} : <>, <i32>` forwards its control
channel's req/ack untouched and drives the data bus with a literal.
Both are wiring: req_out = req_in, ack_in = ack_out, data = VAL.
Zero cells.
Peephole, worth one LUT each: 18 of the 31 are fed directly by a
bare `source`, and source + constant collapse into a single
bd_src #(.W(w), .VAL(v)). The other 13 are triggered by real control
and stay pure wiring.

ops.why: ack = req, and free. Data input ignored.

why: Not a cell: its operands are the function's result channels and it
becomes the generated module's output ports. One per function.

ops.why: Zero-extension is a bus concatenation with constant 0.

why: Sign-extension is a bus concatenation with a replicated top bit.
Absent from the four kernels but heavily present in Dynamatic's own
tests (75 occurrences), so it will appear on other input.

ops.why: Stage 3. The 8-bit adder is the prototype: a carry chain, the one structure this fabric is good at.
Stage 3, same carry chain as addi.
Stage 3, and the deepest logic in the set -- do it after addi works end to end.
Stage 3. The predicate is a bare keyword argument (`cmpi sgt, %a, %b`), not an attribute -- the parser stores it as bracket_arg.
Stage 3, one LUT per bit pair, shallow.
Stage 3, shallow. Absent from the kernels, present in Dynamatic's tests.
Stage 3. Constant shift is a wire; variable shift is a barrel shifter.
Stage 3, logical right shift. Absent from the kernels.

why: Stage 3, NOT bd_mux. handshake.select is a DATA operation: all three
operands arrive, one result leaves, and the unchosen input is still
consumed. bd_mux is a channel operation that leaves the unselected
input's token untouched. Mapping select to bd_mux would silently
leak a token every time. It is a 2:1 datapath multiplexer inside a
compute wrapper -- one LUT3 per bit.
Present in Dynamatic's tests, absent from our kernels because we cut
above --handshake-place-buffers and never run it. Storage stages are
ours to place (COMPILER-PLAN Stage 5), so an incoming `buffer` op is
a hint, not an instruction.
bdc/mem.py's bdc_load_<AW>_<DW>[_seq] station, emit.py's _op_load.
addressResult is absorbed into the owning mem_controller (the
station's own p_addr/p_rdata round trip) and gets no net -- this
table entry is coarse and cannot see that, so it says buildable for
any load whose mem_controller is itself buildable; see mem_controller.
bdc/mem.py's bdc_store_<AW>_<DW>[_seq] station, emit.py's _op_store.
addressResult/dataResult are absorbed the same way load's is. A lone
store's completion (z) is tied off like bd_snk; the first store of a
2-way arbitrated chain instead becomes the second accessor's
program-order token. See mem_controller's caveat: this table cannot
see whether a store's OWN controller is one this backend will
actually emit.
A LOAD-ONLY controller. bdc/mem.py's bdc_memport[_arb]_<AW>_<DW>_<N>,
emit.py's _op_mem_controller. 1 accessor -> plain port; 2 ->
arbitrated port + bd_arbiter + program-order token chain (only the
SECOND accessor is the :seq station -- see bdc/mem.py's own note that
a store's z IS the next access's c, no new cell); >2 raises by name,
no N-way arbiter tree exists.
The guard is what separates this from the store-having entry below,
and it is not arbitrary. A controller owning only loads has one
result per load plus memEnd, and one operand per load plus
memref/memStart/ctrlEnd -- so operands == results + 2. Add a store
and it carries that store's address and data operands plus a
per-block store-count constant, and the identity breaks. No fixed
operand count would do it, because both counts grow with the number
of accesses.
memStart/ctrlEnd/memEnd reproduce dynamatic's own
mem_controller_storeless.v, which hardwires allRequestsDone = 1 --
loads are never tracked for completion. A bd_link holds memStart's
pulse until ctrlEnd arrives and a bd_join #(.N(2)) produces memEnd.
Two cells already on silicon, no new primitive.
That bd_link is deliberately NOT in the cells list above, and this is
load-bearing rather than an oversight: slack.py derives its storage
ops from these lists, and bd_link is a storage cell. Listing it here
declares that a cycle through mem_controller is buffered, which
silences the address-echo cycle checks for both memory kernels --
measured, it dropped fir from 2 unbuffered cycles to 0. The link
sits on the memStart/ctrlEnd control path and offers no capacity to
the address/data cycle slack.py is reasoning about. Same reason
bd_mem itself stays out of STORAGE_CELLS: a station holds its
operands only until the access completes, which is not capacity.
A controller that owns a STORE, and this backend does not build it.
dynamatic's mem_controller_loadless.v gates memEnd on remainingStores
== 0 -- an up/down counter incremented by each block's store-count
token and decremented per completed store. That counter is real
state, it is not a handshake, and there is no clock here to run it
on.
emit.py's _op_mem_controller RAISES by name on this rather than
wiring memEnd without it. Firing memEnd while a store is still in
flight would be a completion signal that reports done early, which
is the same defect class as a null control that fakes its ack --
already paid for once in this project, and it hid real deadlocks
until it was removed.
This entry exists so map.py's verdict matches what emit.py will
actually do. It previously said 'cells' for every controller, which
made --report call single_loop buildable while the emitter refused
it; a status line that reads buildable is believed, and no one reads
the caveat underneath it.

ops.why: Out of scope entirely. Program-order serialisation first, per COMPILER-PLAN Stage 6.
Hardware-instantiation escape hatch for external modules. Rejected loudly until there is a reason to support it.
